laws.title: The Law of Purpose
laws.subtitle: Great Commission clarity drives everything. Make disciples — not crowds, not programs.

heroStat.label: The honest answer
heroStat.text: new converts at AAC in the past year — the gap this Law exists to close.

laws.principle: A high-impact church is not defined by size, music style, or personality. It is defined by three outcomes: lost people coming to Christ, believers growing to maturity, and the church shaping its community.
laws.standfirst: Everything flows from one thing: knowing and committing to the church's God-given mission. The central verb is "make disciples." Not attract crowds. Not run programs. Make disciples.

insights.title: Rethinking what "impact" means
insights.body: Measure impact not by who walks in but by what kind of people walk out. Three markers: lost people coming to Christ, believers maturing, the church influencing its community.

insights.title: The discipleship pipeline
insights.body: Reach the lost → bring them into belonging → mature them in Bible, prayer, family leadership → discover and deploy spiritual gifts → live out the mission in workplace and community → lead others to Christ. Cycle complete.

insights.title: You always get what you measure
insights.body: If your primary metrics are attendance and budget, that is what your culture will optimize for — even unintentionally. High-impact churches measure spiritual growth, evangelism, and leadership reproduction.

insights.title: Vision must be dynamic, simple, local
insights.body: Vision statements must express movement, not description. Short enough to be remembered. Specific enough to anchor the church in its actual community.

insights.title: The research that matters most
insights.body: Christian Schwartz studied 1,000 churches across 32 countries: the single strongest predictor of growth is a church's willingness to seek outside help. Isolation kills growth.

diagnostic.hardTruth: "How many lost people came to Christ this year, and who is specifically nurturing their growth?" Current answer: Zero. That is not condemnation — it is a clarifying crisis. AAC has been in formation mode. It is now time to activate the mission.

coaching.intro: Practical, ground-level tactics from coach Jim Wiegland that translate Chip's principles into AAC's reality.

strategies.name: Discovering people's design
strategies.body: Form a core team of 5+ leaders. Each takes one unengaged person to coffee weekly. Don't recruit them — discover them. Three questions: What are you passionate about? What breaks your heart? What are you naturally gifted at? Where the circles overlap is their design.

strategies.name: Recruiting volunteers
strategies.body: Stand near nursery check-in. Watch for parents who are calm and put-together. Compliment them: "I just want to say — that was neat watching a loving family." Then ask for a micro-commitment: "Would you go in once a month for 20 minutes — tell a story or help with a snack?" Almost no one says no.

strategies.name: Re-engaging volunteers
strategies.body: Volunteer Appreciation Night with free dinner, games, prizes — that's the draw. 10–15 minutes of vision casting embedded in the gratitude. Have key leaders personally call the fringe 50.

strategies.name: Building evangelism culture
strategies.body: Include one evangelism story in every Sunday sermon — even when no conversion happened. "Brother Bill felt led to share the gospel at the grocery store. The man didn't receive Christ yet — but I am so proud of Bill." That is enough. What is rewarded is repeated.

meeting3.name: Equipping for gospel conversations
meeting3.body: Identify your 3–5 "aces" — people gifted at gospel conversations. They exist. Name them. When a less-confident member gets into a deep conversation, they invite "Fred" over: "Hey Fred, come hear what this guy is saying." Rookie watches and prays. Then Fred hands it back.

meeting3.name: Where to take the mission
meeting3.body: Look at your community like an alien from above. Where do strangers naturally talk to strangers? Get in there. The exchange has to be longer than the handout. A backpack takes 3 seconds. A water slide takes 3 hours. West Jefferson Farmers Market is your summer move.

laws.title: The Law of Expectation
laws.subtitle: Pastor's faith — not funding — drives growth. Faith is the lid.

heroStat.label: Schwartz study finding
heroStat.text: predictor of growth across 1,000 churches in 32 countries — the pastor's faith and life.

laws.principle: Christian Schwartz's research across 1,000 churches confirms it: pastor's faith and life are the main growth drivers — not money, space, or staff. Growth is normal, supernatural, and commanded.
laws.standfirst: When Chip shifted his mindset from focusing on barriers to expecting growth, his church doubled. Faith must be reflected in planning, budgeting, and organizing — or you signal "stay small" without saying a word.

insights.title: Pastor's expectation shapes outcomes
insights.body: Faith reflected in planning, budgeting, and organizing. Otherwise the congregation reads the unspoken signal that this church will stay small.

insights.title: Growth is normal, not exceptional
insights.body: Acts shows growth as God's design — thousands added regularly. Early church grew by adapting structure (deacons), not by stalling. Growth requires adapting roles and structure.

insights.title: Supernatural but requires stewardship
insights.body: God alone causes growth. Pastors prepare soil through prayer, teaching, care. The gardening analogy frees pastors from burnout — you don't "make" growth, but you must remove what prevents it.

insights.title: Three growing-pastor traits
insights.body: Commitment to growth as non-negotiable (spiritual, not just numerical). Visionary faith with active prayer life. Effective pastoral leadership.

insights.title: Four barriers to identify and remove
insights.body: Spiritual (sin, pride, lack of integrity). Sociological (relational caps around 100–150). Structural (decentralization needed at 200+). Emotional (the "we're a small church" identity that limits growth).

laws.pullQuote: Churches only grow as far as their leaders' faith and vision allow. Poor leadership caps growth potential.

laws.title: The Law of Design
laws.subtitle: Leaders equip; members minister. The clergy-laity divide must die.

heroStat.label: Chip's warning
heroStat.text: baptisms vs. children — when growth metrics mask the absence of adult conversions.

laws.principle: Pastors equip the saints — they don't do all the ministry. Churches that miss this stagnate around 100. Churches that embrace it multiply.
laws.standfirst: Ephesians 4 and 1 Peter 2 establish the design: every believer is a minister. Pastors are coaches. The pastor doing everything alone is going backwards — limiting growth and burning out.

insights.title: Leaders equip; members minister
insights.body: Growing past 100 requires decentralizing ministry. The pastor who does everything alone limits growth and burns out. God's design has pastors leading and equipping while members serve using their gifts.

insights.title: Biblical foundation: Eph + 1 Peter
insights.body: Ephesians 4:11–12 — Christ gave apostles, prophets, evangelists, pastor-teachers to equip saints for ministry. 1 Peter 2 — every believer is a "living stone" and part of a holy priesthood.

insights.title: No one ministers alone
insights.body: Ministries should be gift-based and team-structured (3–4 people sharing responsibility). New ministry ideas must come back with a committed team, not just an individual initiative.

insights.title: Pastor as coach, not star player
insights.body: Chip's shift from doing ministry alone to equipping others doubled church size in 9 months. Coaching multiplies impact. Investing time in training and coaching beats trying to do all tasks.

insights.title: Growth metrics beyond attendance
insights.body: Real growth = mature disciples making disciples. Chip noted 94 baptisms with 92 being children — flagged the lack of adult conversions. Counting numbers alone can mask lack of real transformation.

laws.pullQuote: The average pastor drives the church backwards — doing everything alone. God's design has the pastor leading and equipping while members minister.

laws.title: The Law of Liberation
laws.subtitle: Discover gifts. Deploy. Get out of the way.

heroStat.label: What lay-led can do
heroStat.text: weekly attendees at Santa Cruz Bible Church when Chip stopped being the star and became the coach.

laws.principle: Growing churches actively train members to discover and use their spiritual gifts — both inside and outside the church. Churches without gift training plateau or decline.
laws.standfirst: Romans 12 establishes interdependent gifting. Every member has a unique role. Pastors who are insecure micromanage — and gifted lay leaders walk away. Pastors who are secure unleash an army.

insights.title: Gift-based ministry drives growth
insights.body: Aligning individual gifts with church purpose — not just filling internal slots — results in lost people coming to Christ, found people maturing, and mature people reproducing.

insights.title: Romans 12 — focus on strengths
insights.body: Spiritual gifts are sovereignly given for God's ordained purposes. Don't fix weaknesses — deploy strengths. Prune outdated ministries that lack gifted, passionate leaders.

insights.title: Pastor as coach, not star
insights.body: Great coaches recruit and organize talent, then unleash them. Empowering lay leaders sparked growth at Santa Cruz Bible Church to 6,500+. High-capacity laypeople bring secular skills the pastor doesn't have.

insights.title: Liberate without control fears
insights.body: Micromanagement drives gifted people away. Focus on doctrinal quality and team health. Allow methods freedom. Accountability should be clear but not stifling.

insights.title: Build a gifts-discovery system
insights.body: Classes, networking systems, or custom tools. Cover motivation, gift identification, ministry fit, deployment. Throw people into ministry quickly — confidence comes from doing.

laws.pullQuote: Liberating gifted people demands overcoming pastoral control fears. Micromanagement drives them away.
